extracted.intended_audience: agency staff, regulated parties, stakeholders, and members of the public participating in federal rulemaking and information-collection reviews
extracted.subtask_short: participation in federal rulemaking and ICR review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how OIRA and OMB review rulemaking and information-collection requests, what standards apply (e.g., Executive Orders and the Paperwork Reduction Act), how the public can participate, and the criteria agencies must meet when proposing regulations or information collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative Procedure Act (APA) requirements for rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The APA governs the process by which Federal agencies propose and establish new regulations and generally requires agencies to provide public notice and seek comment prior to enacting new regulations. It also lays out the process for judicial review of rules in federal court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When issuing proposed and final rules, agencies must publish in the Federal Register; solicit comments on proposed rules; consider public feedback and make appropriate changes; and describe and respond to the public comments in the final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Basic rulemaking process steps
rubrics_metrics.description: Once an agency decides a regulatory action is necessary, it typically develops and publishes a proposed rule in the Federal Register soliciting comments; after considering public feedback and making changes where appropriate, it publishes a final rule with an effective date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The agency must describe and respond to the public comments it received when issuing a final rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of a regulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A regulation is a general statement issued by an agency, board, or commission that has the force and effect of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress often grants agencies the authority or discretion to issue regulations; regulations implement and enforce legislation enacted by Congress by specifying details and requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA's role under Executive Order 12866
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA coordinates interagency Executive Branch review of significant regulations before publication to ensure agency compliance with the principles in Executive Order 12866, including incorporation of public comment, consideration of alternatives, and analysis of costs and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For all significant regulatory actions, EO 12866 requires OIRA review before actions take effect and requires agencies to provide an explanation of the need for the action and an assessment of potential costs and benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 12866 cost–benefit standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies must analyze the costs and benefits of rules and, to the extent permitted by law, act only on the basis of a reasoned determination that the benefits justify the costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should assess both quantitative and qualitative costs/benefits and propose or adopt regulations only upon a reasoned determination that benefits justify costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive Order 13563 principles for regulatory decisionmaking
rubrics_metrics.description: EO 13563 directs agencies to: promote public participation; reduce redundant/inconsistent/overlapping requirements; identify and consider flexible approaches to regulatory problems; promote scientific integrity; and produce plans for retrospective analysis of significant regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: EO 13563 also directs agencies to use best available techniques to quantify anticipated present and future benefits and costs and to consider qualitative values that are difficult to quantify (e.g., equity, human dignity, fairness, distributive impacts). It emphasizes making documents available on regulations.gov and engaging stakeholders before rulemaking is initiated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'significant regulatory action'
rubrics_metrics.description: Under EO 12866 (as amended), regulatory actions are 'significant' if they: (1) have an annual effect on the economy of $200 million or more (adjusted every 3 years); or adversely affect the economy, a sector, productivity, competition, jobs, environment, public health/safety, or governments/communities; (2) create serious inconsistency or interfere with another agency's action; (3) materially alter budgetary impacts of entitlements/grants/user fees/loan programs or rights/obligations of recipients; or (4) raise legal or policy issues for which centralized review would further the President's priorities and the EO's principles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Significant regulatory actions must be reviewed by OIRA before publication in the Federal Register or issuance to the public; OIRA generally designates between 500–700 actions as significant each year.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'economically significant' regulatory action
rubrics_metrics.description: A subset of significant actions: an action is 'economically significant' if OIRA determines it is likely to have an annual effect on the economy of $100 million or more or otherwise materially affect the economy, sectors, jobs, environment, public health/safety, or governments/communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For economically significant regulations, agencies must provide a more detailed assessment of likely benefits and costs, including quantified effects and analysis of potentially effective and reasonably feasible alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose and emphasis of regulatory analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulatory analysis helps agencies anticipate and evaluate likely consequences of rules (costs and benefits), organize evidence on key effects of alternatives, and determine whether benefits justify costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Purposes include learning whether benefits justify costs, promoting accountability to the public, and discovering which alternatives produce the highest net benefits; analysis may show less or more stringent alternatives are appropriate or reveal creative options.

rubrics_metrics.name: OMB's Circular A-4 guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB issues best-practices guidance for regulatory analysis; the latest such guidance is OMB's Circular A-4, 'Regulatory Analysis' (released November 2023).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circular A-4 defines good regulatory analysis and standardizes measurement and reporting of benefits and costs; OMB subjected a draft to peer review and solicited public comments before finalizing.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA review duration limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The period for OIRA review is limited by Executive Order 12866 to 90 days. There is no minimum period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review period may be extended indefinitely by the head of the rulemaking agency; alternatively, the OMB Director may extend the review period on a one-time basis for no more than 30 days.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA return of a rule for reconsideration
rubrics_metrics.description: During OIRA review, the Administrator may send a letter returning the rule for reconsideration if the rule is incompatible with law, analysis is inadequate, the regulation is not justified by the analysis, the rule is inconsistent with EO 12866 or Presidential priorities, or the rule conflicts with other Executive Branch regulations or efforts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A return letter explains why OIRA believes the rulemaking would benefit from further consideration; a return does not necessarily imply OIRA or OMB opposes the draft rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency withdrawal of a rule during OIRA review
rubrics_metrics.description: At any time during OIRA review, an agency may withdraw its rule from review and choose not to move forward or to resubmit after further consideration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interested parties may contact the agency directly with questions regarding specific withdrawals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberative nature of draft documents under review
rubrics_metrics.description: Draft documents under OIRA review are considered deliberative and are not available for public release during review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After a regulatory action is published in the Federal Register, OIRA will make publicly available certain documents exchanged between OIRA and the rulemaking agency during the review period.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA meeting and disclosure policies
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA's policy is to meet with any party interested in discussing issues on a rule under review; meetings must be conducted by the OIRA Administrator or a specific designee and a log of meetings is kept on RegInfo.gov.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA makes public all substantive communications with any party outside the Executive Branch concerning regulatory actions under review: subject, date, participants, and any written material received are disclosed on the OIRA website; after publication, certain exchanged documents are made public.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best ways for outside parties to make ideas known to OIRA
rubrics_metrics.description: The best way to participate is to submit comments directly to the agency during the proposed rule stage, view the Federal Register for notices seeking public comments, and/or file comments via regulations.gov. Parties may also provide written comments to the OIRA Administrator on a regulatory action under review or request a meeting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the EO 12866 Meeting Request page to request a meeting regarding a rule under OIRA review; written comments to OIRA may be provided during specified comment windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reginfo.gov and Regulatory Dashboard purpose and contents
rubrics_metrics.description: RegInfo.gov displays regulatory actions and information collections currently at OIRA for review; the Regulatory Dashboard provides a graphical representation of regulatory actions by agency, length of review, economic significance, and stage of rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If description/abstract for a rule is blank on the Dashboard, it is because the agency did not provide descriptive information in its Unified Agenda entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and purpose of RIN (Regulation Identifier Number)
rubrics_metrics.description: A RIN is assigned by OMB's electronic docketing system to identify each regulatory action listed in the Unified Agenda to make it easier to track the publication history of regulatory actions throughout their development.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB has asked agencies to include RINs in the headings of Rule and Proposed Rule documents when publishing them in the Federal Register.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paperwork Reduction Act (PRA) central requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The PRA provides the statutory framework for Federal collection, use, and dissemination of information, with goals to minimize paperwork/reporting burdens and ensure maximum utility from collected information. It requires agencies to seek public comment on proposed information collections and to submit proposed collections for OMB review and approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Within OMB, OIRA carries out information collection review; the PRA applies to collections using identical questions posed to or reporting/recordkeeping requirements imposed on ten or more 'persons' (individuals, businesses, State/local/Tribal governments) and applies to voluntary and mandatory collections.

rubrics_metrics.name: What counts as an 'information collection'
rubrics_metrics.description: Information includes any statement or estimate of fact or opinion, regardless of form or format (numerical, graphic, narrative; oral or maintained electronically or on paper). Examples include forms (IRS 1040), written reports, surveys, recordkeeping requirements, and third-party/public disclosures (nutrition labeling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The PRA covers collections that use identical questions or impose reporting/recordkeeping on ten or more persons; covers voluntary collections and collections required to obtain Federal benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information Collection Request (ICR) process for OMB approval
rubrics_metrics.description: The agency develops an information collection, publishes a Federal Register notice providing 60 days for public comment, considers comments and makes changes, submits the ICR to OMB and publishes a second notice providing 30 days for comment, and then OIRA concludes its review by approving or taking other actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ICRs related to proposed rules, OMB may 'file comment' instead of approving, instructing the agency to resubmit the ICR at the final rule stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA actions on ICRs and approvals
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA can: Approve, mark as Improperly Submitted, accept Withdrawn, or Disapprove an ICR. OIRA can approve collections for up to three years and may approve with or without change.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an ICR is improperly submitted, OIRA returns it if procedural requirements are not met; if OIRA disapproves an ICR, the agency may not proceed with the collection and 'no person shall be subject to any penalty for failing to comply' with it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emergency review for ICRs
rubrics_metrics.description: Under certain circumstances, the PRA authorizes an agency to request 'emergency' review and approval by OMB where normal processes would result in public harm or are not possible because of an unanticipated event.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When granting emergency review, the agency must explain the reason and take all practicable steps to consult with members of the public; OMB may modify or waive public comment requirements in these situations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria OMB evaluates during review of proposed collections
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB evaluates whether the collection is necessary for the proper performance of agency functions (practical utility); minimizes Federal information-collection burden (especially on those most adversely affected); and maximizes practical utility and public benefit from information collected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA also reviews consistency with applicable laws, regulations, and policies related to privacy, confidentiality, security, information quality, and statistical standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to participate in the information-collection review process
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the public are encouraged to monitor sponsoring agency Federal Register notices seeking comments on information collections and provide feedback; they may also submit comments to sponsoring agencies and OIRA about any currently approved collections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments can be submitted to OIRA during the first 30 days of the information-collection review via the View ICR - Agency Submission page; a list of ICRs open for public comment is available on the Information Collection Review page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidential Business Information (CBI) rules for comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not submit information whose disclosure is restricted by statute (trade secrets, commercial/financial information) to www.reginfo.gov. Comments submitted through www.reginfo.gov cannot be claimed as CBI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments received through the website will waive any CBI claims for the information submitted.

rubrics_metrics.name: How OIRA will use and publish submitted comments
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA considers public comments during review of ICRs. Electronic comments submitted through Reginfo.gov will be maintained in ROCIS and OIRA is the official custodian. Information and materials submitted may be seen by various people; personally identifiable information included in comments may be publicly disclosed on Reginfo.gov.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments submitted online will not be publicly disclosed on Reginfo.gov until OIRA concludes its review. Only comments verified by OIRA will be publicly disclosed when review is completed. Contact info provided with comments submitted online will not be publicly disclosed on Reginfo.gov and may only be used by OIRA. Reginfo.gov offers public data in XML format which may include commenter info if included in the posted submission.

rubrics_metrics.name: ICR Dashboard types and meanings
rubrics_metrics.description: The ICR Dashboard displays seven types of information-collection requests: New collection; Revision; Extension without change; Reinstatement without change; Reinstatement with change; Existing collection in use without OMB Control Number; and Discontinue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Definitions: Revision = substantive revision; Extension without change = extend approval at least every 3 years; Reinstatement categories allow reuse of prior OMB Control Numbers; Existing collection in use without OMB Control Number = agency begun collection; Discontinue = agency asks OMB to discontinue approval. Non-material/non-substantive changes are considered technical/ministerial and do not require public comment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information available on viewing an information collection
rubrics_metrics.description: When viewing an information collection on Reginfo.gov, users can see basic info (title, burden hours) and can click OMB Control Number or ICR Reference Number to learn more; OMB Control Number shows OMB review history, ICR Reference Number can show collection instruments and supporting documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An exception: ICRs created or revised due to an associated proposed or final regulation are not made public until OMB's review is completed and the rules are published in the Federal Register.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA's role in Executive Branch privacy policy
rubrics_metrics.description: OIRA (within OMB) assists Federal agencies on privacy matters, develops Federal privacy policy, and oversees implementation of privacy policy by agencies, with authority from laws including the Privacy Act of 1974, the PRA, and the E-Government Act of 2002.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OIRA's oversight includes privacy, confidentiality, security, information quality, and statistical standards as part of ICR review.
